title: Star and Crescent Emoji ☪️ Meaning: Islam, Ramadan and Eid
description: The star and crescent emoji ☪️ is widely recognized as a symbol of Islam. See how it is used for Ramadan, Eid and Muslim identity, and how it differs from 🌙 and 🕌.
summary: The ☪️ star and crescent emoji is the most widely recognized symbol associated with Islam. Muslims use it in Ramadan and Eid greetings and to express their identity, and it appears in interfaith messages. It also appears on the national flags of several countries, including Turkey, Pakistan and Malaysia.
meaning: In everyday use ☪️ means "Muslim" or "Islamic." People put it in profiles to show their faith, add it to greetings like "Ramadan Mubarak" and "Eid Mubarak," and use it in posts about mosques, fasting and community events. Outsiders use it in respectful holiday wishes to Muslim friends and colleagues.

The symbol's history is more political than scriptural. The crescent and star were used in the region long before Islam and became strongly associated with the Ottoman Empire, whose flag carried them. From there they spread to the flags of many Muslim-majority countries. Islam itself has no official symbol, and some Muslims prefer not to treat the crescent as one, but it remains the most widely understood visual shorthand.

The moon does have real religious weight. The Islamic calendar is lunar, and the sighting of the new crescent marks the start and end of Ramadan and the dates of the two Eids. That is part of why ☪️ and 🌙 cluster around the fasting month and the celebrations that follow.

The emoji is not a generic moon-and-star picture. Using it for bedtime, the night sky or astrology will read as a religious reference. For those, 🌙 and ✨ say night without the religious association. In Muslim-majority countries the emoji may also appear in patriotic posts because of the flags, though the religious reading still comes first for most readers.

contexts.label: During Ramadan and Eid
contexts.body: The heaviest use comes with the fasting month: "Ramadan Kareem ☪️," iftar invitations, suhoor jokes at 4am, and then Eid al-Fitr greetings at its end. It returns for Eid al-Adha, which coincides with the Hajj pilgrimage. Brands and schools use it in holiday notices for Muslim customers and students.

contexts.label: In bios and identity
contexts.body: A ☪️ in a bio identifies the person as Muslim, often next to a country flag. Some users prefer 🕋 or a line of Arabic, such as "Alhamdulillah," because of the debate about the crescent's status. Either way, the emoji is understood as a statement of faith.

contexts.label: In interfaith messages
contexts.body: Church groups, schools and public figures include ☪️ with ✝️ and ✡️ in messages of solidarity or peace among religions, especially after attacks on places of worship. Christian neighbors also send it with Eid greetings. In these contexts it should be used with the occasion clearly named.

examples.text: Ramadan Mubarak to everyone fasting this month ☪️🌙
examples.meaning: A greeting at the start of Ramadan.

examples.text: Eid Mubarak! Thank you for the food, auntie ☪️❤️
examples.meaning: Eid greetings and thanks for a holiday meal.

examples.meaning: An invitation to break the fast together after sunset.

examples.text: Praying for the victims and their families ☪️✝️✡️
examples.meaning: An interfaith message of sympathy after a tragedy.
A bio line listing faith as part of personal identity.

combos.meaning: Ramadan or the moon sighting that begins and ends it.
The mosque, congregational prayer, or community events.
Dua, the Islamic posture of supplication with open palms.
Eid celebrations after Ramadan or during the Hajj season.

confusedWith.difference: 🌙 is just the moon and can mean night, sleep or dreams. It is also used for Ramadan. ☪️ adds the star and reads specifically as a symbol of Islam.
🕌 shows a domed mosque with minarets and refers to the place of worship. ☪️ is the abstract symbol. Many people pair them in Ramadan and Friday prayer posts.
🕋 depicts the Kaaba in Mecca, the direction of prayer and the center of the Hajj. It is more specifically sacred than ☪️, which is a widely used emblem rather than a holy site.

avoid: Do not use ☪️ as a decorative night-sky or goodnight symbol; 🌙 or ✨ fits that.
Avoid it in jokes or arguments that mock Muslims or Islam.
Do not assume every Muslim considers it the symbol of their faith; some prefer other markers.
design: A crescent moon with a five-pointed star set inside its curve. On most platforms it appears in white on the purple tile shared by religious symbols. It is an older text character, so in some fonts it shows as a plain black symbol. The orientation of the crescent and the star's position are consistent across major vendors.

faqs.q: Is ☪️ an official symbol of Islam?
faqs.a: Not in a doctrinal sense. Islam has no official emblem, and the star and crescent came into wide use through the Ottoman Empire and later national flags. It is nonetheless the most widely recognized symbol associated with Muslims today.

faqs.q: How can I tell ☪️ and 🌙 apart?
faqs.a: 🌙 is a plain crescent moon and can mean night, sleep or Ramadan. ☪️ includes a star and specifically refers to Islam. For a religious greeting, either works; for goodnight, use 🌙.

faqs.q: Which flags have a star and crescent?
faqs.a: Several, including Turkey, Pakistan, Malaysia, Algeria, Tunisia and Azerbaijan. The emoji itself is not a flag, and in messages it is read as a religious symbol rather than a reference to any one country.

faqs.q: Is it okay for non-Muslims to use ☪️?
faqs.a: Yes, when the use is respectful, such as wishing a Muslim friend Eid Mubarak or showing solidarity. It should not be used as a casual decoration or to stereotype.

faqs.q: When was the star and crescent emoji added?
faqs.a: The character existed as a text symbol well before emoji. It was given emoji presentation in 2014 and is listed under Emoji 0.7, together with other religious symbols.
